Becoming a Theory Wonk: Notes, Proofs and Pain Overture

Becoming a Theory Wonk: Notes, Proofs and Pain Lachlan Astfalck 2025-10-22 Overture I have no formal education in the mathematical sciences and have, for the most part, learned these topics by myself, and often by mistake. In trying to understand the machinery that underpins modern statistics, I found myself attempting to learn all of mathematics at once: analysis, probability, topology, measure theory, and the list goes on. Unsurprisingly, this approach was both inefficient and confusing. Over time, I realised I needed a single place to organise the ideas that recur in my work and studies. This document is that attempt: an incomplete and evolving encyclopedia of mathematical notions that I’ve found myself returning to. The focus here is on mathematical statistics, that dark crevice of mathematics too applied for the pure mathematicians, and too theoretical for the applied statisticians. The exposition is informal and unapologetically tailored to my own needs. When I include proofs, I do so with more steps and commentary than one might find in a standard textbook. Perhaps I’m slow, but the tersity of proofs confined to print media often assumes an ability greater than mine. For the moment, I have grouped these writings under the following loose banners. Mathematical statistics is messy and does not follow a linear progression, but rather is a braid of ideation. As such, certain topics are difficult to allocate, and where this is the case I have put them where I best understand them. Analysis - The study of the machinery that makes calculus behave. Nothing statistical lives here, but the tools built in analysis quietly underpin nearly everything we do later. Linear Algebra and Functional Analysis — The language of vectors and transformations at infinity. The unspoken grammar of modern statistics. Measure Theory - The formal machinery for assigning ‘size’ to sets and probability to events. Often needlessly abstract, but undeniably elegant. Once you surrender to probability as a measure, you can ignore the ‘frequentist vs Bayesian’ noise. Statistical Asymptotics - The study of what happens to estimators and models when the data grow without bound. A necessary fiction of rigour and delusion. Weakly Dependent Processes - Time series and spatial processes that cling to independence just tightly enough to ruin your assumptions, but loosely enough to claim asymptotic validity.

Pro maioribus Everything that I’ve learnt has come from one of the many remarkable monographs and texts that others have written. What follows is a selection of those that I recommend without hesitation to anyone wishing to understand these ideas more deeply. The statistical analysis of time series. Anderson, TW (1971). Whilst notionally a book about time series, it is really about much more. I picked it up to understand the covariance structure of the periodogram and found, instead, a first glimpse into the rich mathematical world that underpins so much of what we take for granted in statistical modelling. Asymptotic statistics. Van der Vaart, AW (2000). This book is the reason these notes exist: it is proof that brilliance and accessibility rarely coincide. This is the book that made me want to know more, but didn’t slow down to help. These notes are the record of me, painfully, figuring it out. Linear algebra done right. Axler, S (2024). I wish this was how I was taught linear algebra. Axler replaces the rote manipulation of matrices with an emphasis on structure, abstraction, and proof. The book is an antidote to every course that began with Gaussian elimination and never recovered.

Compactness A subset \(\mathbb{K} \subset \mathbb{X}\) of a metric space \((\mathbb{X}, d)\) is compact if every open cover of \(\mathbb{K}\) has a finite subcover. An open cover is any collection of open sets \(\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}\) such that \[ \mathbb{K} \subset \bigcup_{\alpha \in A} U_\alpha, \] meaning that each point of \(\mathbb{K}\) lies inside at least one of the \(U_\alpha\). A subcover is a smaller collection of these sets that still covers \(\mathbb{K}\). Compactness says “whenever you try to cover \(\mathbb{K}\) with (possibly infinitely many) open sets, a finite selection will do the job.” Personally, I find this one of those overly mathematical notions that I’m sure exists for good reason, but it typically suffices just to say “its compact”, and to live your life. Compactness quietly guarantees that local properties can be made global, and that limits behave well inside bounded regions. Example: Closed and Bounded Euclidean Space In Euclidean space, a set is compact if and only if it is both closed and bounded. Again, it’s a silly math game; normal people would just think, of course it does, just pick the interval, plus minus a little bit, make it open, job done. Alas, mathematicans demand more. Without loss of generality I’ll show this for the interval \([0,1]\). Let \(\mathcal{U} = \{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}\) be an open cover of \([0,1]\). We don’t have to do more than this with this assumption, \(\mathcal{U}\) just has to exist. Define \[ S = \{\, x \in [0,1] : [0,x] \text{ can be covered by finitely many sets from } \mathcal{U}\,\}. \] That is, \(S\) is a set of all of the points up to which we can achieve finite coverage between \([0,1]\). First, note that \(S\) is nonempty since \(0 \in S\) as you can always cover a point with an open set that bounds it. Next, note that the set is bounded above by \(1\). Let \(s = \sup S\). Assume, for contradiction, that \(s < 1\). Because \(\mathcal{U}\) covers \([0,1]\), there exists some \(U_{\alpha_0} \in \mathcal{U}\) such that \(s \in U_{\alpha_0}\). As \(U_{\alpha_0}\) is open, there exists \(\eta > 0\) with \((s - \eta, s + \eta) \subset U_{\alpha_0}\). This means we can cover a bit beyond \(s\) using the same set \(U_{\alpha_0}\). By the definition of \(s\) as a supremum (i.e. maximum), for any \(\eta>0\) there exists \(x\in S\) with \(s-\eta/2<x\le s\). Intuitively, \(x\) is a point just short of \(s\) that we can already reach with finitely many sets. Since \(x\in S\), the segment \([0,x]\) can be covered by finitely many members of \(\mathcal{U}\); denote this finite subcover by \(\mathcal{V}\subset\mathcal{U}\). Because \(s\) lies in the open set \(U_{\alpha_0}\), there exists \(\eta>0\) such that \((s-\eta,s+\eta)\subset U_{\alpha_0}\), so this same open set covers a little interval past \(s\). Hence \[ [0,\min\{1,s+\eta/2\}]\subset \left\{[0,x] \cup U_{\alpha_0}\right\}. \] The right-hand side is the union of finitely many sets from \(\mathcal{U}\) (those in \(\mathcal{V}\) together with \(U_{\alpha_0}\)) so \([0,\min\{1,s+\eta/2\}]\) is finitely covered. This contradicts the definition of \(s\) as the least upper bound of \(S\), because it shows that a point larger than \(s\) can also be finitely covered. Therefore \(s=1\). Use Case: Lebesgue Number Theorem One useful place I find myself envoking compactness is justifying the existence of a finite rectangular cover. This can be justified by the Lebesgue Number Theorem. The Theorem states: Let \((\mathbb{X}, d)\) be a compact metric space and let \(\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}\) be an open cover of \(\mathbb{X}\). Then there exists a number \(\lambda > 0\) (called a Lebesgue number for the cover) such that for every subset \(S \subset \mathbb{X}\) with \(\mathrm{diam}(S) < \lambda\), \[ S \subset U_\alpha \quad \text{for some } \alpha \in A. \] In particular, every ball \(B(x, \lambda)\) of radius \(\lambda\) around any point \(x \in \mathbb{X}\) is contained in at least one member of the cover. Corollary (Finite Rectangular Cover). Let \(I \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) be a compact rectangle and \(\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}\) an open cover of \(I\). Then there exists \(\lambda > 0\) such that any closed rectangle \(R \subset I\) with side lengths less than \(\lambda / \sqrt{n}\) satisfies \[ R \subset U_\alpha \quad \text{for some } \alpha. \] Consequently, \(I\) can be partitioned into finitely many such rectangles \(\{R_j\}\), each contained in some \(U_\alpha\). Compactness ensures the existence of a global “small enough” scale \(\lambda\) that works uniformly across the space. Once \(\lambda\) is known, we can subdivide a compact region into finitely many smaller boxes of diameter less than \(\lambda\), knowing that each box will fit entirely inside one of the open sets of the cover.

Uniform Continuity Let \(f : \mathbb{X} 	o \mathbb{Y}\) be a function between metric spaces \((\mathbb{X}, d_1)\) and \((\mathbb{Y}, d_2)\), where \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) measure distance over the input and output spaces respectively. The function \(f\) is uniformly continuous if, for every \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists some \(\delta > 0\) such that for all \(x_1, x_2 \in \mathbb{X}\), \[ d_1(x_1, x_2) < \delta \quad \Rightarrow \quad d_2(f(x_1), f(x_2)) < \epsilon. \] I sometimes think of uniform continuity as box continuity: for any box of height \(\epsilon\) centred at any point \(x \in \mathbb{X}\), there exists a width \(\delta\) such that the graph of \(f\) always exits the box through the sides, never the top. Wikipedia has a nice graphic of this. Infimum and Supremum The infimum and supremum generalise the notion of minima and maxima in real-valued sets. They give us upper and lower boundaries without requiring the endpoints to actually exist in the set. The infimum (or greatest lower bound) is the largest number that is still less than or equal to every element of the set. The supremum (or least upper bound) is the smallest number that is still greater than or equal to every element of the set. If these bounds happen to be part of the set, then it’s just the usual maximum or minimum. (Don’t be a try-hard and write \(\inf\) and \(\sup\) in your mathematics when dealing with discrete or finite sets.) Formally, for a set \(A \subset \mathbb{R}\) \(u = \sup A\) if \(a \le u\) for all \(a \in A\), and for every \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists some \(a \in A\) with \(a > u - \epsilon\). \(l = \inf A\) if \(l \le a\) for all \(a \in A\), and for every \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists some \(a \in A\) with \(a < l + \epsilon\). For instance, if \(A = (0,1)\), then \(\inf A = 0\) and \(\sup A = 1\). I always forget which is which. Noting the latin derivations help: infimum from infimus (inferior) and supremum from supremus (superior). In fact, in older texts (such as Billingsly) these are often directly called the limits inferior and superior.

Portmanteau Lemma The Portmanteau Lemma is a collection of deceptively simple results that quietly underpins much of modern asymptotic theory. The name portmanteau (its adjective definition, “consisting of a wide range of things that are considered as a single thing”) is apt: the lemma gathers several equivalent formulations of weak convergence of probability measures. It’s houses a lot of technical machinery that lets us move freely between convergence of probabilities, expectations, and indicator functions. Portmanteau Lemma (as per van der Vaart). Let \(X_n\) and \(X\) be random elements taking values in a metric space \((\mathcal{X}, d)\). The following are equivalent: \(X_n \xrightarrow{d} X\), i.e., \(\P(X_n \in A) \to \P(X \in A)\) for all continuity points of \(x \mapsto \P(X \leq x)\); \(\E[f(X_n)] \to \E[f(X)]\) for all bounded, continuous functions \(f\); \(\E[f(X_n)] \to \E[f(X)]\) for all bounded, Lipschitz functions \(f\); \(\lim \inf \E[f(X_n)] \geq \E[f(X)]\) for all nonnegative, continuous functions \(f\); \(\lim \inf \P(X_n \in G) \geq \P(X \in G)\) for every open set \(G\); \(\lim \sup \P(X_n \in F) \leq \P(X \in F)\) for every closed set \(F\); \(\P(X_n \in B) \to \P(X \in B)\) for all Borel sets \(B\) with \(\P(X \in \partial B) = 0\) where \(\partial B\) is the boundary of \(B\). Proofs (1) This is the definition of weak convergence (or convergence in distribution). In effect the rest imply that they are equivalent conditions. Note, the phrasing “for all continuity points” means “the \(x\) where the limiting CDF \(F_X(x) = \P(X \leq x)\) is continuous”. This is sufficient for convergence in distribution and avoids pathologies at discontinuities.
